subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If f is the function defined by f(x) = (x − 1)/(√x − 1) for x > 1, f(x) = 5 − 3x for −2 ≤ x ≤ 1, and f(x) = 6/(x − 10) for x < −2, then discuss the continuity of f.

mark_split.label: Check each piece on its own interval

NOTE ON THE ANSWER: f is continuous at x = 1 (left limit, value and right limit all 2) and NOT continuous at x = −2 (left limit 6/(−12) = −1/2, value and right limit both 11). steps.label: Check each piece on its own interval
steps.margin_note: First mark. The question says discuss, so the open intervals have to be dealt with as well as the junctions. Each piece is shown to be continuous by naming what it is and where its own formula could fail.
steps.memory_tip: Here the three pieces meet at two junctions. At every other point f is continuous, because its formula there is a polynomial or a quotient of continuous functions with a non-zero denominator.

steps.why: The word discuss asks for the whole real line, not one point. Showing continuity on the three open intervals first reduces the rest of the question to two junction tests.
common_mistakes: Checking only x = 1 and never testing x = −2.
Claiming 6/(x − 10) is discontinuous on (−∞, −2) because it is a fraction, when x = 10 is not in that interval.

steps.label: Test the junction x = 1
steps.margin_note: Second mark. x = 1 belongs to the middle piece, because −2 ≤ x ≤ 1 carries the equals sign. The right-hand formula gives 0/0 at 1, so it must be simplified before the limit is taken.
steps.memory_tip: x − 1 = (√x)² − 1², so it factorises as (√x − 1)(√x + 1) — a difference of two squares, with √x in place of x.

steps.why: The right-hand formula is 0/0 at x = 1, so it cannot be substituted. Writing x − 1 as a difference of two squares cancels the factor that is zero at x = 1 and turns the limit into a substitution.
common_mistakes: Substituting x = 1 into (x − 1)/(√x − 1) and writing 0/0 as the right limit.
Taking f(1) from the piece x > 1, when x = 1 is not in that interval.
lines_compact: All three are 2, so f is continuous at x = 1.

steps.label: Test the junction x = −2
steps.margin_note: Third mark. x = −2 also belongs to the middle piece, so the value and the right limit agree automatically. The left limit comes from 6/(x − 10) and is the number that makes the test fail.
steps.memory_tip: At x = −2 the denominator is −2 − 10 = −12. Both numbers are negative, so they combine to −12, not to −8 or 8.
lines: and lim(x → −2) f(x) does not exist.

recall.must_convey: That the left limit at −2 is 6/(−12) = −1/2 while f(−2) and the right limit are both 11, so f is not continuous there.

steps.why: The two one-sided limits are computed from different formulas, so they have no reason to agree. Showing both numbers is what proves the failure rather than asserting it.
common_mistakes: Taking f(−2) from 6/(x − 10), when x = −2 belongs to the middle piece.
Computing 5 − 3(−2) as 5 − 6 = −1 by dropping the sign of the negative input.
lines_compact: and lim(x → −2) f(x) does not exist.

steps.margin_note: Last mark. The verdict has to cover the whole line: three open intervals plus the two junctions, one of which passes and one of which fails. A yes or a no alone is not enough here.
steps.memory_tip: For a discuss question, write the verdict as everywhere except the listed points — that form covers the whole line in one line.

steps.why: The question asks for a discussion of continuity, so the answer is a description of the whole domain, not a yes or a no. Stating that f is continuous at every real number except the one failing point is the complete answer.
common_mistakes: Answering only that f is not continuous, without saying where.
Listing x = 1 as a point of discontinuity because two formulas meet there, when the test passes.
